I hosted a group of 3 newcomers this weekend to walk them through their first build session.

One brought an HGBF Gundam Portent, one a MG Shin Musha Gundam, and the other a MG Astray Blue Frame Second L.

I started work on a MG Buster Gundam alongside them.

They did a pretty good job for their first time around, the one with the Gundam Portent did the best of group, and actually finished the model in the first session, with pretty solid nub control and panel lining for a first timer.

The Shin Musha builder was actually more concerned about plastic damage from sanding than they were with nubs, so I'm going to work on demonstrating top coating with them for next time, and go over sanding and finishing again to hopefully get them to break that concern early.

The astray builder would still be sitting here if I didn't stop him. He was really in to it, it was great watching him fall in like that. His nub control needs work. He'll definitely be back for next session.

I got the torso of the Buster assembled during that session. It's been a fun kit so far, pretty good to demonstrate basics for the group. I'll apply some decals next week, and do a top coating demonstration.

Hello fellow bass players. I've been thinking I'd like to run 2 heads to have a bit more control over my tone. Just wondering if any of you guys do this? What do you have each head doing- one for high frequency one for low frequency? Do you run the same heads or different ones? Any advice is appreciated.
I've never done it myself but read about a pedal for such a thing.
You can also get an A/B/Y splitter so you can run both heads at the same time.
One head for high frequency and one for low is usually the way to go. My Rick splits neck and bridge pickups, and I actually run my bridge pickup through an old Gibson M-20.

I have a Carvin R1000 that bi-amps...that is I have a crossover built into the pre-amp section to send different content to separate internal power amps that can run to different cabs. This doesn't allow for, say, running a dirt box on the higher frequencies and a clean signal on the lows but a decent pedal can make this sort of magic happen. Dirt cheap head for what it does and saves me the bother of lugging around other gear as a good enough compressor, noise gate and a wide range of EQing is built right in. For the $320usd I paid for the head plus a 4x10 plus horn cab I'm a very happy camper. (with one cab the head bridges the two power amps and sends a stronger signal to my 4x10 and that's plenty enough for me and my needs.)

Very late to the party, but I used to do this with a splitter. Ran one head clean, and the other one with distortion. It worked pretty well for the particular sound I was trying to get at the time, but I don't use it anymore.
